title: Cosmic Cycles and World Ages: Cyclical and Linear Conceptions of Time Across Civilizations
description: Human civilizations have developed profoundly different conceptions of time and cosmic history. Some traditions envision time as cyclical -- an eternal recurrence of creation, degeneration, destruction, and renewal -- while others conceive of time as linear, moving irreversibly from a definite beginning toward an ultimate consummation. Many traditions combine elements of both. The cyclical model predominates in South Asian, Mesoamerican, and ancient Greek thought; the linear model is most fully developed in Zoroastrian, Jewish, Christian, and Islamic traditions. This file compares seven major systems of cosmic time, examining their structures, durations, mechanisms of transition, and philosophical implications.

systems.name: Yugas (The Four World Ages)
systems.source_text: The Mahabharata (Shanti Parva and Vana Parva); the Laws of Manu (Manusmriti, c. 2nd century BCE - 2nd century CE); the Vishnu Purana (c. 4th-5th century CE); the Bhagavata Purana (c. 9th-10th century CE); the Surya Siddhanta (astronomical text, c. 4th-5th century CE). The yuga system is elaborated most fully in the Puranic literature.

ages.name: Satya Yuga (Krita Yuga)
ages.description: The Golden Age of truth, virtue, and spiritual perfection. Dharma stands on all four legs (the bull of dharma metaphor). Humans are naturally virtuous, long-lived (100,000 years), and in direct communion with the divine. No disease, no social hierarchy, no need for governance. Meditation is the primary spiritual practice.

ages.name: Treta Yuga
ages.description: The Silver Age. Dharma stands on three legs -- virtue has declined by one quarter. Rituals and sacrifices become necessary for spiritual progress. Kingdoms, social hierarchy, and warfare emerge. The avatar Rama appears in this age. Lifespan: 10,000 years.

ages.name: Dvapara Yuga
ages.description: The Bronze Age. Dharma stands on two legs -- virtue has declined by half. Disease, discord, and suffering increase. The Vedas are divided into four (by Vyasa). The avatar Krishna appears at the end of this age. The Mahabharata war marks its close. Lifespan: 1,000 years.

ages.name: Kali Yuga
ages.description: The Dark Age, the current age, which began in 3102 BCE (traditional dating, associated with the death of Krishna). Dharma stands on one leg. Virtue is at its minimum; greed, hypocrisy, conflict, and spiritual ignorance prevail. Sacred knowledge is forgotten, rulers are corrupt, and social bonds dissolve. Lifespan: 100-120 years. The Kali Yuga ends with the appearance of the Kalki avatar, who destroys the wicked and inaugurates a new Satya Yuga.

systems.current_age: Kali Yuga (began 3102 BCE; approximately 5,128 years into a 432,000-year cycle as of 2026 CE)
systems.total_duration: One Mahayuga (complete cycle of four yugas) = 4,320,000 years. One thousand Mahayugas = one Kalpa (Day of Brahma) = 4,320,000,000 years. One Day of Brahma plus one Night of Brahma (during which the universe is dissolved) = 8,640,000,000 years. Brahma's lifespan = 100 Brahma-years = 311,040,000,000,000 years. After Brahma's death, a Maha-Pralaya (Great Dissolution) occurs, followed by a new Brahma and a new cosmic cycle.
systems.mechanism_of_transition: Progressive moral and spiritual degeneration drives the transition from one yuga to the next. At the nadir of the Kali Yuga, the avatar Kalki (the tenth avatar of Vishnu) appears on a white horse, destroys the forces of adharma, and ushers in a new Satya Yuga. The cycle then repeats. The transitions between yugas include twilight periods (sandhya and sandhyamsha) during which the characteristics of the outgoing and incoming ages overlap.
systems.golden_age_concept: The Satya Yuga (also called Krita Yuga) is the golden age of perfect dharma, truth, and spiritual realization. It is both a past paradise and a future promise: the cycle guarantees that after the darkness of the Kali Yuga, the golden age will return. Some Hindu reformers (notably Sri Aurobindo) reinterpreted the yuga cycle as a progressive evolution rather than a degeneration.

systems.name: Kalpas and Cosmic Cycles
systems.source_text: The Agganna Sutta (Digha Nikaya 27, Pali Canon); the Visuddhimagga (Buddhaghosa, 5th century CE); the Abhidharmakosha (Vasubandhu, 4th-5th century CE); the Kalachakra Tantra (Vajrayana Buddhism). The Buddha's cosmological teachings are found scattered throughout the Pali Canon and systematized in Abhidharma literature.

ages.name: Vivartakalpa (Evolving/Formation Aeon)
ages.description: The period during which a world-system (lokadhatu) comes into being. After the dissolution of the previous cosmos, beings from the Abhassara (Radiant) Brahma realm begin to descend, initially as luminous, ethereal beings who gradually become denser, more material, and more differentiated. Social distinctions, agriculture, property, and governance emerge progressively.

ages.name: Vivattatthayi Kalpa (Continuing/Abiding Aeon)
ages.description: The period during which the world-system exists and sentient beings inhabit it. This includes cycles of moral improvement and decline. During moral high points, human lifespans extend to 80,000 years; during moral nadirs, they shrink to 10 years. Buddhas appear during the declining phase when lifespans are in a middle range.

ages.name: Samvartakalpa (Dissolving/Destruction Aeon)
ages.description: The period of cosmic destruction, occurring through one of three means: fire (consuming everything up to the first jhana Brahma realm), water (up to the second jhana realm), or wind (up to the third jhana realm). Sentient beings are reborn in higher realms before the destruction of the lower realms.

ages.name: Samvattathayi Kalpa (Void Aeon)
ages.description: The period after destruction and before the next formation, during which the lower realms are empty. Only the higher Brahma realms continue to exist. This corresponds to the primordial void between cosmic cycles.

systems.current_age: We are in the Vivattatthayi Kalpa (Abiding Aeon) of the current world-system, during a period of moral decline (human lifespans decreasing). The current kalpa is called the Bhadrakalpa (Auspicious Aeon) because five Buddhas appear in it; Shakyamuni was the fourth, and Maitreya will be the fifth.
systems.total_duration: One Mahakalpa (complete cycle of four kalpas) is incalculably long. The Buddha compared a kalpa to the time it would take to wear away a mountain of granite by brushing it once every hundred years with a silk cloth. The Abhidharmakosha gives one kalpa as approximately 1,347,000,000 years (16,800,000 intermediate kalpas). The number of past Mahakalpas is beginningless (anamatagga).
systems.mechanism_of_transition: Cosmic cycles are driven by the collective karma of sentient beings. Moral degeneration leads to cosmic contraction and destruction; the positive karma of beings in higher realms seeds the next cycle of formation. The process is entirely impersonal -- there is no divine creator or destroyer. The Buddha emphasized that the number of past lives and past cosmic cycles is 'without discoverable beginning' (Samyutta Nikaya 15.3), far exceeding human comprehension.
systems.golden_age_concept: At the beginning of each world-system's abiding period, beings are luminous, ethereal, and blissful (recalling the Satya Yuga). As they consume material food and develop craving, they become denser and more conflicted. The golden age is not a stable paradise but the first phase of an inevitable decline. However, the appearance of Buddhas provides the possibility of individual liberation from the cycle entirely (nibbana/nirvana), which transcends the cosmological cycles altogether.

systems.name: Ages of Man (Metallic Ages)
systems.source_text: Hesiod, Works and Days (c. 700 BCE), lines 109-201; Ovid, Metamorphoses (c. 8 CE), Book I. Hesiod's account is the earliest surviving Greek version. Plato's Statesman (268d-274e) presents a different cyclical cosmology in which the cosmos alternates between periods of divine guidance and divine withdrawal.

ages.name: Golden Age (Genos Chryseon)
ages.description: Under the rule of Kronos. Humans lived like gods, free from toil, sorrow, and old age. The earth produced food spontaneously. There was no war, no injustice, no need for laws. Humans died peacefully, as if falling asleep, and became benevolent daimones (spirits) guarding mortals.

ages.name: Silver Age (Genos Argyreon)
ages.description: Inferior to the Golden Age. Humans were childish, living a hundred years in infancy before a brief, troubled adulthood. They were arrogant and refused to worship the gods. Zeus destroyed them, and they became blessed spirits of the underworld.

ages.name: Bronze Age (Genos Chalkeon)
ages.description: Humans were fierce, warlike, and violent, obsessed with bronze weapons and warfare. They destroyed themselves through their own aggression and descended to the cold House of Hades without honor.

ages.name: Heroic Age (Genos Heroon)
ages.description: A departure from the metallic scheme -- this is the age of the demigod heroes, including the warriors of Thebes and Troy. Nobler and more just than the Bronze Age, these heroes were sent to the Isles of the Blessed after death. This insertion reflects the importance of Homeric epic in Greek culture.

ages.name: Iron Age (Genos Sidereon)
ages.description: The current age. Humans are burdened with toil, suffering, and moral corruption. Fathers and children are at odds; guest-right is violated; might makes right. Hesiod laments: 'Would that I had not been born in this age, but either earlier or later.' The Iron Age will end when Aidos (Shame) and Nemesis (Righteous Indignation) depart from the earth, leaving humanity to its destruction.

systems.current_age: The Iron Age (Hesiod explicitly places himself and his audience in this age)
systems.total_duration: Unspecified for individual ages. The Stoics later developed a fully cyclical cosmology (ekpyrosis) in which the cosmos is periodically consumed by fire and reborn identically (the 'eternal return'), with each cycle lasting a 'Great Year' of approximately 26,000 years (or, in some versions, much longer).
systems.mechanism_of_transition: Moral degeneration drives the transition from age to age. Each successive race is less virtuous, less happy, and more violent than the last (with the exception of the Heroic Age, which is an interpolation). The gods create each new race; Zeus destroys or allows the destruction of each degenerate race. The Stoic eternal return, by contrast, is driven by cosmological necessity: the divine fire (Logos) periodically reabsorbs all matter and then recreates the cosmos identically.
systems.is_cyclical: Partially. Hesiod's account is primarily linear and degenerative (from Gold to Iron), though the Stoics later imposed a fully cyclical framework. Plato's Statesman suggests a cyclical alternation between periods of divine guidance and cosmic drift.
systems.golden_age_concept: The Golden Age (Kronos's reign) is the archetypal paradise of effortless prosperity, moral purity, and communion with the divine. It profoundly influenced Roman literature (Virgil's Fourth Eclogue prophesied its return), Christian millennial thought, and the Western utopian tradition. The myth encodes a pessimistic philosophy of history: the present is a degradation of a more perfect past.

systems.name: Five Suns (Nahui Ollin)
systems.source_text: The Legend of the Suns (Leyenda de los Soles, c. 1558); the Aztec Sun Stone (Piedra del Sol, c. 1479 CE); Bernardino de Sahagun, Historia General de las Cosas de Nueva Espana (Florentine Codex, c. 1545-1590); the Codex Chimalpopoca. Accounts vary across Aztec and broader Nahua sources.

ages.name: Nahui Ocelotl (Four Jaguar / First Sun)
ages.description: Presided over by Tezcatlipoca (Smoking Mirror). Inhabitants were giants who were devoured by jaguars when the sun was destroyed. This age lasted 676 years (13 x 52-year cycles).

ages.name: Nahui Ehecatl (Four Wind / Second Sun)
ages.description: Presided over by Quetzalcoatl (Feathered Serpent). Destroyed by hurricanes; inhabitants were transformed into monkeys. Lasted 364 years (7 x 52).

ages.name: Nahui Quiahuitl (Four Rain / Third Sun)
ages.description: Presided over by Tlaloc (Rain God). Destroyed by a rain of fire (volcanic eruption or divine fire); inhabitants were transformed into turkeys, butterflies, or dogs. Lasted 312 years (6 x 52).

ages.name: Nahui Atl (Four Water / Fourth Sun)
ages.description: Presided over by Chalchiuhtlicue (Jade Skirt, goddess of water). Destroyed by a great flood; inhabitants were transformed into fish. One human couple survived by hiding in a hollow log. Lasted 676 years (13 x 52).

ages.name: Nahui Ollin (Four Movement / Fifth Sun)
ages.description: The current age, presided over by Tonatiuh (the Sun God). This sun was created at Teotihuacan when the god Nanahuatzin sacrificed himself by leaping into a great bonfire, becoming the sun. The other gods sacrificed themselves to set the sun in motion. This age will end in catastrophic earthquakes. The 52-year cycle renewal (New Fire Ceremony / Toxiuhmolpilia) was performed to prevent the premature end of the Fifth Sun.
ages.duration: Ongoing; destined to end in earthquakes

systems.current_age: Nahui Ollin (Four Movement / Fifth Sun), created at Teotihuacan through divine self-sacrifice
systems.total_duration: Each sun lasts several hundred years (multiples of the 52-year calendar cycle). The total duration of all five suns is approximately 2,028 years (in some accounts), though numbers vary across sources. The 52-year cycle (xiuhmolpilli) structures Aztec temporal reckoning.
systems.mechanism_of_transition: Each age is destroyed by a specific cataclysm (jaguars, wind, fire, flood, earthquakes) associated with one of the four elements and a presiding deity. The destruction of each sun is driven by divine conflict and cosmic instability. The Fifth Sun requires continuous sustenance through human blood sacrifice (nextlahualli, 'the sacred debt') to Tonatiuh, without which the sun will cease to move and the age will end. This cosmological framework provided the theological justification for Aztec ritual sacrifice.
systems.golden_age_concept: The Aztec system does not have a straightforward 'golden age' concept. Each sun is different rather than progressively worse. The current Fifth Sun is the age of humanity's greatest flowering but also the most precarious, sustained only by the ongoing cosmic debt of sacrifice. The creation of the Fifth Sun through Nanahuatzin's self-immolation establishes sacrifice as the foundational cosmic principle: the world exists because the gods gave their lives, and humans must reciprocate.

systems.name: World Ages and Ragnarok
systems.source_text: The Poetic Edda, especially Voluspa (The Seeress's Prophecy); the Prose Edda (Snorri Sturluson, c. 1220 CE), especially Gylfaginning. The Voluspa is the single most important source for Norse eschatology.

ages.name: The Current World Age
ages.description: The age that began with the creation of the cosmos from Ymir's body and the creation of Ask and Embla. It encompasses the entire span of human and divine history, including the construction of Asgard, the adventures of the gods, and the progressive signs of cosmic degeneration. The current age is characterized by increasing conflict, moral decay, and the weakening of the bonds that restrain cosmic evil (the wolf Fenrir is bound by the fetter Gleipnir; the Midgard Serpent encircles the world; Loki is bound with the entrails of his son).

ages.name: The Age After Ragnarok
ages.description: After the apocalyptic destruction of Ragnarok, a renewed, purified world emerges from the sea. The surviving gods (Vidar, Vali, Modi, Magni, Hoenir, and the returned Baldr and Hodr) gather in the meadows of Idavoll. A new human couple, Lif and Lifthrasir, emerge from their hiding place in Hoddmimir's Wood, having survived on morning dew. The new world is green, fertile, and peaceful. A new, unnamed 'mighty one' descends from above to rule all.

systems.ragnarok_narrative: Ragnarok (the Doom or Twilight of the Gods) begins with the Fimbulwinter -- three successive winters with no intervening summer. Moral chaos prevails among humans (the Axe Age, the Sword Age, the Wind Age, the Wolf Age). Brothers kill brothers; all bonds of kinship dissolve. The wolf Fenrir breaks free and swallows the sun. The Midgard Serpent rises from the ocean, flooding the land. Loki breaks free and leads the forces of chaos -- the fire giant Surtr, the ship Naglfar crewed by the dead, the frost giants -- against the gods. In the final battle: Odin is swallowed by Fenrir; Thor kills the Midgard Serpent but dies from its venom after nine steps; Freyr falls to Surtr; Heimdall and Loki kill each other; Tyr and the hound Garm kill each other. Surtr sets the world ablaze. The earth sinks into the sea. Then, the purified earth rises again.
systems.current_age: The current world age, prior to Ragnarok (though some sources suggest the signs of approaching Ragnarok are already visible)
systems.total_duration: Unspecified. The Norse sources do not give numerical durations for cosmic ages. The emphasis is on the qualitative character of the ages rather than their quantitative measurement.
systems.mechanism_of_transition: Progressive cosmic entropy: the bonds constraining evil weaken, moral order collapses, and the forces of chaos (giants, monsters, fire) overwhelm the forces of order (the Aesir gods). Ragnarok is not a punishment but the inevitable working out of the cosmic process. The destruction is total but not final: the renewed world that emerges is purified and perfected.
systems.is_cyclical: Ambiguously so. The Voluspa describes a single cycle: creation, degeneration, destruction, renewal. Whether the cycle repeats infinitely is not explicitly stated in the sources, though some scholars (notably Mircea Eliade) interpret it as implicitly cyclical. The influence of Christian eschatology on the medieval Icelandic sources makes it difficult to distinguish pre-Christian cyclical elements from imported linear-apocalyptic elements.
systems.golden_age_concept: The early period of the current age, when the gods played at golden tables (gullnar toflor) in the meadows of Idavoll, represents a brief golden age before the arrival of giantesses and the corruption of the world. The post-Ragnarok world represents a more definitive golden age: Baldr returns from Hel, the earth produces unsown crops, and all evils are healed. The golden tablets are found again in the grass -- a symbol of the return to original perfection.

systems.name: The Three Ages and Cosmic Renovation (Frashokereti)
systems.source_text: The Gathas (Old Avestan hymns of Zarathustra, c. 1200-900 BCE); the Younger Avesta (Vendidad, Yashts); the Bundahishn (Book of Primal Creation, Middle Persian, c. 9th century CE); the Denkard (Acts of Religion, c. 9th century CE). The fully developed cosmological system appears primarily in the Middle Persian (Pahlavi) texts.

ages.name: Bundahishn (Creation)
ages.description: Ahura Mazda creates the world in a perfect, spiritual (menog) state, then manifests it in material (getig) form. The creation includes the sky (an egg-shaped shell of stone), water, earth, plants, the Primordial Bull (Gavaevodata), and the First Man (Gayomart). The world exists in a state of perfect goodness, with no death, disease, or suffering.

ages.name: Gumezishn (Mixture)
ages.description: Angra Mainyu (Ahriman), the Hostile Spirit, attacks the good creation, introducing death, disease, pollution, and moral evil. The primordial bull and first man die, but from their remains come all species of animals and all humanity respectively. The current world is the arena of the cosmic struggle between Ahura Mazda (Truth/Asha) and Angra Mainyu (Falsehood/Druj). Three saviors (Saoshyants) appear at 1,000-year intervals to progressively renew the world.
ages.duration: 6,000 years (from Angra Mainyu's attack to the final renovation)

ages.name: Wizarishn (Separation/Renovation/Frashokereti)
ages.description: The final separation of good from evil and the complete renovation (frashokereti) of the world. The last savior (Saoshyant Astvat-ereta) appears, the dead are resurrected, all souls pass through a river of molten metal (which purifies the wicked and feels like warm milk to the righteous), Angra Mainyu is defeated and destroyed forever, and the world is restored to its original perfection -- but now permanently, with no possibility of further corruption. The material world is glorified, not abolished.
ages.duration: 3,000 years culminating in the eternal perfected world

systems.current_age: The age of Mixture (Gumezishn), during which the cosmic battle between good and evil is ongoing in every dimension of existence
systems.total_duration: 12,000 years in the standard Zoroastrian schema (3,000 + 6,000 + 3,000), though some texts extend this. The period is divided into four 3,000-year segments, each associated with specific cosmic events and the appearance of a savior figure.
systems.mechanism_of_transition: The cosmic struggle between Ahura Mazda and Angra Mainyu drives history toward its predetermined conclusion. Every morally good thought, word, and deed by humans strengthens the forces of Asha (Truth) and hastens the final renovation. Every evil act strengthens Druj (Falsehood) and delays it. The three Saoshyants (born from the miraculously preserved seed of Zarathustra) appear at crucial junctures to turn the tide. Human moral agency is thus cosmically significant: the outcome is assured, but human participation is essential.
systems.golden_age_concept: The original creation (Bundahishn) is the initial perfect state, and the Frashokereti (final renovation) restores and surpasses it. Zoroastrian time is decisively linear: it begins with a perfect creation, passes through a period of cosmic struggle, and culminates in an eternal perfection that can never be undone. This linear-eschatological framework profoundly influenced Jewish, Christian, and Islamic conceptions of history, apocalypse, resurrection, and the Last Judgment.

systems.name: The Great Year (Magnus Annus) and Eternal Return
systems.source_text: Chrysippus and Cleanthes (Stoic fragments, 3rd century BCE, preserved in Diogenes Laertius, Plutarch, and others); Marcus Aurelius, Meditations (c. 170-180 CE); Plato, Timaeus (39d: the 'perfect year' when all celestial bodies return to their original positions); Nietzsche, The Gay Science (1882) and Thus Spoke Zarathustra (1883-1885) -- modern philosophical revival of eternal return.

ages.name: The Cosmic Cycle (Diakosmesis)
ages.description: The cosmos exists as an ordered, living whole governed by the Logos (divine reason/fire). It proceeds through a fixed course from its fiery origin (ekpyrosis -- cosmic conflagration) through a period of differentiation (diakosmesis) in which the elements separate, the world forms, and sentient beings live out their fated lives. When the Great Year is complete, the cosmos is reabsorbed into the divine fire, and then the entire cycle repeats identically, down to the smallest detail. Every individual, every event, every thought recurs exactly as before, infinitely.
ages.duration: Estimates varied: some Stoics calculated the Great Year as approximately 10,800 years; others as 36,000 years (based on the precession of the equinoxes); Heraclitus mentioned 10,800 years. The Timaeus associates the 'perfect year' with the return of all celestial bodies to their original alignment.

systems.current_age: We are within one iteration of the eternal cosmic cycle, at an indeterminate point between one ekpyrosis and the next
systems.total_duration: Each cycle is finite (10,800-36,000 years, depending on the source), but the number of cycles is infinite. There is no first cycle and no last cycle. The Stoic universe is eternal in both directions.
systems.mechanism_of_transition: The cosmic fire (divine Logos) periodically reabsorbs all differentiated matter through ekpyrosis (cosmic conflagration), then re-emanates the cosmos in precisely the same form. The process is governed by inexorable fate (heimarmene) -- the causal chain of the Logos working itself out with absolute determinism. There is no possibility of deviation: each cycle is identical to every other in every detail.
systems.golden_age_concept: The Stoic system does not have a golden age in the degenerative sense. Each cycle is identical; there is no decline from a better past. The closest analog is the state of pure fire/Logos before differentiation (which some Stoics identified with Zeus in his purest state). Nietzsche's revival of eternal return transforms the concept into an existential test: amor fati (love of fate) -- the ability to affirm one's life so completely that one would will its eternal recurrence -- is the mark of the Ubermensch.
